entry.content:
DDPM from a Score Perspective

In DDPM , we know that

\[x_t\sim q(x_t|x_0) = N(x_t; \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_t} x_0, (1 - ar{\alpha}_t) I) ag{1}\]

According to Tweedie’s Formula, we can obtain:

\[\sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_t} oldsymbol{x}_0 = oldsymbol{x}_t + (1 - ar{\alpha}_t) abla_{x_t} \log p( oldsymbol{x}_t) ag{2}\]

Tweedie’s Formula:

For a Gaussian variable $z\sim \mathcal N(z;\mu_z,\Sigma_z)$, we have

\[\mu_z=z+\Sigma_z abla_z\log p(z)\]

Meanwhile, from (1) we know

\[x_t=\sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_t}x_0+\sqrt{1- ar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon_t\]

Substituting into (2), we obtain

\[ abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)=- rac{\epsilon_t}{\sqrt{1- ar{\alpha}_t}}\]

Thus

\[ egin{align*} oldsymbol{\mu}_q &= rac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{x}_t - rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{1 - ar{\alpha}_t} \sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t\ &= rac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{x}_t + rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \color{red} abla_{x_t} \log p( oldsymbol{x}_t) \end{align*}\]

Similarly, we model the reverse process as

\[ egin{align*} oldsymbol{\mu}_{ heta} &= rac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{x}_t - rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{1 - ar{\alpha}_t} \sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{ heta}(x_t,t)\ &= rac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} oldsymbol{x}_t + rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} \color{red}s_{ heta}(x_t,t) \end{align*}\]

Therefore, we transform the estimation of $\epsilon_t$ and $\epsilon_{ heta}$ in DDPM into the estimation of $ abla\log p(x)$, which gives

\[ egin{align*} &\arg\min_{ heta} D_{ ext{KL}} \left( q( oldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \vert oldsymbol{x}_t, oldsymbol{x}_0) \parallel p_{ heta}( oldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \vert oldsymbol{x}_t) ight) \ =& \arg\min_{ heta} rac{1}{2\sigma_q^2(t)} \left[ \lVert oldsymbol{\mu}_{ heta} - oldsymbol{\mu}_q Vert_2^2 ight] \ =& \arg\min_{ heta} rac{1}{2\sigma_q^2(t)} \left[ \left\lVert rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} s_{ heta}( oldsymbol{x}_t, t) - rac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} abla \log p( oldsymbol{x}_t) ight Vert_2^2 ight] \ =& \arg\min_{ heta} rac{1}{2\sigma_q^2(t)} rac{(1 - \alpha_t)^2}{\alpha_t} \left[ \color{red}\lVert s_{ heta}( oldsymbol{x}_t, t) - abla \log p( oldsymbol{x}_t) Vert_2^2 \color{black} ight] \end{align*}\]

Hence, we find that the optimization objective of DDPM is actually consistent with Score-Based Models, both estimating the score function.

We further compare the optimization objective of DDPM:

\[L_t = \mathbb{E} \left[ rac{(1 - \alpha_t)^2}{2\alpha_t (1 - ar{\alpha}_t) \sigma^2} \color{red}\left\| oldsymbol{\epsilon}_t - oldsymbol{\epsilon}_ heta \left( x_t, t ight) ight\|_2^2 \color{black} ight]\]

We note that when $L_t$ reaches its optimum, we have

\[\epsilon_{ heta}(x_t,t)=\mathbb E ig[\epsilon_t|x_t,t ig]=\mathbb E ig[\epsilon_t|x_0,t ig]\]

This indicates that the model actually learns the mean of the noise given data $x_0$. In other words, the conditional expectation learned by our network already contains information about the true sample $x_0$, which is what enables us to obtain the distribution of true data by learning the noise.

Meanwhile, we find that under optimal conditions, $L_t$ cannot reach 0, meaning that our optimization objective does not achieve maximum likelihood between the predicted distribution and the true distribution (otherwise the loss should reduce to 0). Combined with Score-Based Models, we know this is because we are actually predicting the score of the data distribution, and there is still a certain gap between the score distribution and the data distribution.

SDE Model

What happens if we extend the finite steps $T$ to infinite steps? Experimental validation shows that larger $T$ can yield more accurate likelihood estimates and better quality results. Thus, continuous-time perturbation of data can be modeled as a stochastic differential equation (SDE).

Definition

There are many forms of SDEs. One form given by Dr. Yang Song in his paper ) (which can be considered a Diffusion-Type SDE, requiring coefficients to depend only on time t and current value x) is:

\[\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{x} = f( oldsymbol{x}, t)\mathrm{d}t + g(t)\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{w}\]

where $f(\cdot)$ is called the drift coefficient, $g(t)$ is called the diffusion coefficient, $ oldsymbol{w}$ is a standard Brownian motion, and $\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{w}$ can be viewed as white noise. The solution to this stochastic differential equation is a set of continuous random variables $\lbrace oldsymbol x(t) brace_{t\in [0,T]}$, where $t$ represents the continuous version of the discrete form $(1, 2, \ldots, T)$.

We use $p_t( oldsymbol{x})$ to denote the probability density function of $ oldsymbol{x}(t)$, which corresponds to the previous $p_{\sigma_t}( oldsymbol{x}_t)$. Here $p_0( oldsymbol{x}) = p( oldsymbol{x})$ is the original data distribution, and $p_T( oldsymbol{x}) = \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})$ is the white noise obtained after noise perturbation.

Brownian Motion

If a stochastic process $\lbrace X(t), t \geq 0 brace$ satisfies:

  • $X(t)$ is an independent increment process;
  • $ orall s, t > 0, X(s + t) - X(s) \sim N(0, c^2 t)$

then the stochastic process $\lbrace X(t), t \geq 0 brace$ is called Brownian motion (denoted as $B(t)$) or Wiener process (denoted as $W(t)$). In this text, we will subsequently denote it as $W(t)$. If $c = 1$, it is called standard Brownian motion, satisfying $W(t) \sim N(0, t)$.

Forward SDE

We can directly discretize the equation

\[\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{x} = f( oldsymbol{x}, t)\mathrm{d}t + g(t)\mathrm{d} oldsymbol{w}\]

where

\[ egin{aligned} dx & o x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t\ dt & o \Delta t\ dw & o w(t+\Delta t)-w(t)\sim\mathcal N(0,\Delta t)=\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon \end{aligned}\]

Thus, the discrete form of the SDE is represented as:

\[\color{red} x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t=f(x,t)\Delta t+g(t)\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon\]

where $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$.

VE-SDE

For NCSN, the forward process (adding noise) is shown as follows:

\[ egin{aligned} x_t &= x_0+\sigma_t\epsilon\ x_{t+\Delta t} &= x_t+\underbrace{\sqrt{\sigma_{t+\Delta t}^2-\sigma_t^2}}_{\color{red}\sqrt{ rac{\sigma_{t+\Delta t}^2-\sigma_t^2}{\Delta t}}\sqrt{\Delta t}}\epsilon \end{aligned}\]

Therefore, in the corresponding SDE representation

\[ egin{aligned} f(x_t,t) &= 0\ g(t) &= \lim\limits_{\Delta o 0}\sqrt{ rac{\sigma_{t+\Delta t}^2-\sigma_t^2}{\Delta t}}=\sqrt{2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t} \end{aligned}\]

The corresponding continuous SDE for the VE process is:

\[\color{blue}dx=\sqrt{2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t}dW\]

VP-SDE

For DDPM, its forward process is represented as follows:

\[ egin{aligned} x_t &= \sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_t}x_0+\sqrt{1- ar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon\ x_{t+1} &= \sqrt{1- eta_{t+1}}x_t+\sqrt{ eta_{t+1}}\epsilon \end{aligned}\]

We continualize the discrete time $1,2,\cdots,t,\cdots T$ to $[0,1]$, i.e., let

\[ egin{aligned} t & o rac{t}{T}=t'\ 1 & o rac{1}{T}=\Delta t \end{aligned}\]

We can also let $ eta_{t’}=T eta_t$, thus

\[ egin{align*} x_{t'+\Delta t}&=x_{t+1}=\sqrt{1- eta_{t+1}}x_t+\sqrt{ eta_{t+1}}\epsilon\ &=\sqrt{1- eta_{t'+\Delta t}\Delta t}\cdot x_{t'}+\sqrt{ eta_{t'+\Delta t}\Delta t}\cdot \epsilon\ &= ig(1- rac{1}{2} eta_{t'}\Delta t ig)x_{t'}+\sqrt{ eta_{t'}}\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon \end{align*}\]

Therefore, in the corresponding SDE representation, we have

\[ egin{aligned} f(x_t,t) &= - rac{1}{2} eta_{t'}x_t\ g(t) &= \sqrt{ eta_{t'}} \end{aligned}\]

The corresponding continuous SDE for the VP process is:

\[\color{blue}dx=- rac{1}{2} eta_{t'}x_tdt+\sqrt{ eta_{t'}}dW\]

We expect that when $t o T$, the image becomes pure noise, then $\sigma_t o\infty$, but $ ar{\alpha}_t o 0$ is sufficient. This requires that in NCSN, the variance of noise gradually expands, while in DDPM, the noise variance remains between $(0,1)$. Therefore, they are respectively called VE-SDE and VP-SDE.

Reverse SDE

Using the discrete forward SDE, we can derive its reverse process. From the forward SDE:

\[\color{red} x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t=f(x,t)\Delta t+g(t)\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon\]

we have the conditional probability:

\[x_{t+\Delta t}|x_t\sim \mathcal{N}(x_t+f(x_t,t)\Delta t, g^2(t)\Delta tI)\]

Considering the reverse process from $x_{t+\Delta t}$ to $x_t$, we have the conditional probability:

\[ egin{align*} p(x_t|x_{t+\Delta t})&= rac{p(x_{t+\Delta t}|x_t)p(x_t)}{p(x_{t+\Delta t})}\ &=p(x_{t+\Delta t}|x_t)\exp(\log p(x_t)-\log p(x_{t+\Delta t}))\ &\approx p(x_{t+\Delta t}|x_t)\exp\{\color{red} -(x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)-\Delta t rac{\partial}{\partial t}\log p(x_t) \color{black}\}\ &\propto \exp\{ - rac{\|x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t-f(x_t,t)\Delta t\|_2^2}{2g^2(t)\Delta t} - (x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)-\Delta t rac{\partial}{\partial t}\log p(x_t) \}\ &=\exp igg\{ - rac{1}{2g^2(t)\Delta t}\|(x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t)- ig[f(x_t,t)-g^2(t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) ig]\Delta t\|_2^2 - \Delta t rac{\partial}{\partial t}\log p(x_t)- rac{f^2(x_t,t)\Delta t}{2g^2(t)}+ rac{\|f(x_t,t)-g^2(t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) \|_2^2\Delta t}{2g^2(t)} igg\}\ &\stackrel{\Delta t o 0}{=} \exp igg\{ - rac{1}{2g^2(t)\Delta t}\| (x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t)- ig[f(x_t,t)-g^2(t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) ig]\Delta t \|_2^2 igg\} \end{align*}\]

Therefore, $x_t|x_{t+\Delta t}$ follows a Gaussian distribution with mean and variance as follows:

\[ egin{aligned} \mu &= x_{t+\Delta t}- ig[f(x_t,t)-g^2(t) abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) ig]\Delta t\ \sigma^2 &= g^2(t)\Delta t \end{aligned}\]

Thus, we can obtain both the discrete and continuous forms of the reverse SDE process:

\[x_{t+\Delta t}-x_t= ig[f(x_t+\Delta t,t+\Delta t)-g^2(t+\Delta t) abla_{x_t+\Delta t}\log p(x_{t+\Delta t}) ig]\Delta t+g(t+\Delta t)\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon\] \[\color{blue}dx= ig[f(x_t,t)-g^2(t)\color{red} abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)\color{blue} ig]dt+g(t)dW\]

Therefore, after we have learned the score function, the reverse process becomes completely solvable. During generation, we start by sampling $x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, and gradually obtain $x_0$ using the discrete process above. This discretization method for stochastic differential equations is also called the Euler–Maruyama method.

For NCSN, its forward VE process continuous SDE is:

\[\color{blue}dx=\sqrt{2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t}dW\]

Then its reverse process is:

\[dx=-2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)dt+\sqrt{2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t}dW\]

Written in discrete form, it becomes

\[x_t-x_{t-1}=-2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)\Delta t+\sqrt{2\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t}\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon_t\]

In the case where $\sigma_t\dot\sigma_t=1$, if we set $\Delta t=\delta$ (this is done only for formal consistency, without real meaning), then we have

\[x_{t-1}=x_t+2\delta abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)+\sqrt{2\delta}\epsilon\]

This also unifies with the Langevin Equation mentioned earlier.

Optimization Target

Solving the reverse SDE requires us to know the terminal distribution $p_T( oldsymbol{x})$ and the score function $ abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \log p_t( oldsymbol{x})$. By design, the former is close to the prior distribution $\pi( oldsymbol{x})$, which is fully tractable.

To estimate $ abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \log p_t( oldsymbol{x})$, we train a time-dependent score-based model $s_ heta( oldsymbol{x}, t)$ such that $s_ heta( oldsymbol{x}, t) \approx abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \log p_t( oldsymbol{x})$. This is similar to NCSN’s $s_ heta( oldsymbol{x}, i)$, which after training satisfies $s_ heta( oldsymbol{x}, i) \approx abla_{ oldsymbol{x}} \log p_{\sigma_i}( oldsymbol{x})$.

Our training objective for $s_ heta( oldsymbol{x}, t)$ is a continuous weighted combination of Fisher divergences, given by :

\[\mathbb{E}_{t \in \mathcal{U}(0,T)} \mathbb{E}_{p_t(\mathbf{x})} \left[ \lambda(t) \left\| abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_t(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{s}_ heta(\mathbf{x}, t) ight\|_2^2 ight]\]

Relationship with Likelihood

When $\lambda(t)=g^2(t)$, under some regularity conditions, there exists an important connection between our weighted combination of Fisher divergences and the KL divergence from $p_0$ to $p_ heta$:

\[ egin{align*} \mathrm{KL}(p_0(\mathbf{x}) \| p_ heta(\mathbf{x})) &\leq rac{T}{2} \mathbb{E}_{t \in \mathcal{U}(0,T)} \mathbb{E}_{p_t(\mathbf{x})} \left[ \lambda(t) \| abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_t(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{s}_ heta(\mathbf{x}, t) \|_2^2 ight] \ &+ \mathrm{KL}(p_T \| \pi) \end{align*}\]

Due to this special connection with KL divergence, and the equivalence between minimizing KL divergence and maximizing likelihood in model training, we call $\lambda(t)=g(t)^2$ the likelihood weighting function. Using this likelihood weighting function, we can train score-based generative models to achieve very high likelihoods.

Probability Flow ODE

We can transform any SDE into an ODE without changing the marginal distributions $\lbrace p_t(x) brace_{t\in[0,T]}$ of the stochastic differential equation. Therefore, by solving this ODE, we can sample from the same distribution as the Reverse SDE. The ODE corresponding to the SDE is called the Probability flow ODE, with the form:

\[\color{blue}dx= ig[f(x_t,t)- rac{1}{2}g^2(t)\color{red} abla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)\color{blue} ig]dt\]

The figure below depicts trajectories of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and probability flow ordinary differential equations (ODEs). It can be seen that ODE trajectories are significantly smoother than SDE trajectories, and they transform the same data distribution into the same prior distribution and vice versa, sharing the same set of marginal distributions $\lbrace p_t( oldsymbol{x}) brace_{t\in[0,T]}$. In other words, trajectories obtained by solving the probability flow ODE have the same marginal distributions as SDE trajectories.

Using probability flow ODEs provides many benefits:

  1. Exact likelihood computation
  2. Manipulating latent representations
  3. Uniquely identifiable encoding
  4. Efficient sampling

Conditional Generation

According to Bayes’ theorem

\[p(x|y)= rac{p(x)p(y|x)}{p(y)}\]

Taking the score with respect to $x$ on both sides gives

\[ abla_x\log p(x|y)= abla_x\log p(x)+ abla_x\log p(y|x)\]

Both latter terms are score functions that we can estimate. Therefore, we can generate $p(x|y)$ by solving the reverse SDE.
entry.summary: This post explores the unification of DDPM and Score-based Models in diffusion generative modeling. We show how x-prediction and score-prediction are fundamentally equivalent, and how both can be viewed through the lens of Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs).
